newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's Moslems, Croats agree on joint army.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's Moslems, Croats agree on joint army.

text.p: Bosnia's Croats and Moslems, former enemies turned federal partners, have taken final steps to form a joint army after a long-stalled process, a U.S. envoy said on Wednesday.

Ambassador James Pardew, charged by the White House with overseeing a U.S.-backed military programme for the federation, told reporters top Moslem and Croat officials had signed orders to appoint the commander and joint command of the federal army.
"The agreement constitutes final approval of these (military) organisations and now allows critical appointments to be made," Pardew told reporters in Sarajevo.

But German diplomat Christian Schwartz-Schilling, a political mediator for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, warned on Wednesday that relations inside the federation look like a war "not fought by weapons but all civil means".

After visiting the southern town of Bugojno, where authorities have blocked the return of refugees expelled in 1993, Schwartz-Schilling told reporters that Moslem and Croat leaders were playing "foolish games" to retain power on the territory they control.

Negotiations to form a municipal council elected in September in Moslem-controlled Bugojno have failed completely and the mediator said he would give up the issue unless a high-level accord was reached.

Croats and Moslems waged war in 1993-94 before bowing to U.S. pressure and forming the federation. But the deal has never moved much beyond agreements on paper because of narrow nationalist agendas and mistrust on both sides.

Under Wednesday's military accord, the commander of the Moslem-led Bosnian army, General Rasim Delic, becomes head of the joint command. Croat General Zivko Budimir will be his deputy and the chief-of-staff.
The orders were signed by Alija Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, and Kresimir Zubak, the Croat member of the presidency.
Federal military officials had asked international donors for $6.2 million for the purchase of a laser system used to simulate effects of weapons for combat training.
